reference.source: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry; DSM-5-TR
clinicalPearls: The disorder develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, with symptoms arising and lasting from three days up to one month after the trauma
Symptoms span intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal, including intrusive memories, distressing dreams, flashbacks, and a sense of unreality or detachment
If characteristic symptoms persist beyond one month, the diagnosis is reconsidered as post-traumatic stress disorder rather than acute stress disorder
Dissociative features such as depersonalisation, derealisation, or amnesia for part of the event can be prominent in the acute aftermath
Many people exposed to trauma recover without progressing to a chronic disorder, so the diagnosis helps identify those at higher risk who may benefit from early support
Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy is the recommended intervention, whereas single-session psychological debriefing is not beneficial and may be harmful
Medication has a limited role, mainly for specific symptoms such as severe sleep disturbance, and benzodiazepines are generally avoided
Assess suicide risk and provide practical support, safety, and psychoeducation as part of early management
reference.pathophysiology: Acute stress disorder reflects the immediate dysregulation of fear and stress-response systems following trauma, with heightened amygdala-driven threat processing, altered prefrontal regulation, and disturbed hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and noradrenergic activity. Impaired encoding and contextualisation of the traumatic memory, together with dissociative responses, are thought to underlie the intrusive and dissociative symptoms, modulated by prior vulnerability and severity of exposure.
additionalDifferentials: Post-traumatic stress disorder once symptoms exceed one month
Adjustment disorder in response to a stressor
Panic disorder or other anxiety disorders
Traumatic brain injury or medical sequelae of the event
Brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor
additionalInvestigations: Clinical interview characterising the traumatic exposure and symptom onset
Medical evaluation for injuries or head trauma related to the event
Screening for comorbid depression and substance use
redFlags: Suicidal or self-harm ideation following the trauma
Ongoing exposure to danger, such as continuing abuse or violence
Severe dissociation impairing safety or the ability to seek help
Concurrent physical injury or head trauma requiring medical attention
reference.prognosis: Many individuals with acute stress disorder recover within weeks, but a significant proportion progress to post-traumatic stress disorder, and the acute diagnosis identifies people who may benefit from early, evidence-based support. Prognosis is better with early trauma-focused intervention, safety, and social support, and worse with severe or ongoing trauma, prominent dissociation, and prior psychiatric illness.
pitfalls: Providing single-session psychological debriefing, which is ineffective and potentially harmful
Prescribing benzodiazepines, which may impair recovery
Assuming all acutely distressed trauma survivors will develop a chronic disorder
Overlooking suicide risk or ongoing danger to the patient
Missing concurrent physical or head injury from the traumatic event
management: Offer trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy as the first-line intervention for those with significant or persistent symptoms
Provide practical psychological first aid, safety and psychoeducation, avoiding single-session psychological debriefing, which is unhelpful and potentially harmful
Address acute sleep disturbance and hyperarousal with sleep-focused measures, avoiding routine benzodiazepine use given dependence risk and poorer trauma outcomes
Undertake structured suicide risk assessment and safety planning, and evaluate for head injury or physical trauma sustained during the event
Monitor the symptom course and reclassify as post-traumatic stress disorder if characteristic symptoms persist beyond one month
Identify and treat comorbid depression and substance misuse
Refer to specialist mental health services when symptoms are severe, escalating or associated with risk
